## How VS Code finds R

Nothing in my synced settings names an R version or a path:

- `r.consolePath` is `"radian"`, found on `PATH`.
- `r.executablePath` is not set, so vscode-R uses `R.exe` on `PATH`, which is rig's shortcut in `C:\Program Files\R\bin`.
- The R Debugger extension reads only the old `r.rpath.windows`. That is not set either, so it also uses `R.exe` on `PATH`. vscode-R shows a one-time warning about this whenever R Debugger is installed; without a project pin there is nothing to do.
- radian also starts the R on `PATH`, unless `R_HOME` is set or `--r-binary` is given.

So the R version is whatever `rig default` says on that machine. The settings stay identical everywhere, which is what lets [Settings Sync](profiles_sync.qmd) carry them.

## Switch R for the whole machine

```powershell
rig list              # installed versions; * marks the default
rig add release       # install the newest release (or: rig add 4.5)
rig default 4.6.2     # use it everywhere
```

Then open a new R terminal. No VS Code change is needed. Remember that a new R version starts with an empty package library: install the [R packages](install.qmd#the-r-packages) for it.

## Pin one project to a version

Sometimes a project needs an older R, for example one whose `renv.lock` was made with R 4.5.1. The pin goes into that project's workspace settings, `.vscode/settings.json`, which override the profile.

### With the R Version Switcher extension

I wrote (well, vibe-coded) a small extension for this: [**R Version Switcher**](https://github.com/OndrejMottl/r-version-switcher). It works with rig and the R extension. It is not on the Marketplace; install the `.vsix` from its [latest release](https://github.com/OndrejMottl/r-version-switcher/releases/latest) with `code --install-extension r-version-switcher-1.2.0.vsix --profile R`. Its commands:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| **R: Switch Version** | Pick an installed R version for this workspace. The list marks the current one, the system default and the one in `renv.lock`. |
| **R: Use R Version from renv.lock** | Switch to the version recorded in `renv.lock`; offers to install it (or the newest patch of the same minor version) if it is missing. |
| **R: Show Current Version** | The workspace's R version and path, and whether the path is valid. |
| **R: Add Version** / **R: Remove Version** | `rig add` / `rig rm`, run as a VS Code task so you see the output. |
| **R: Set System Default Version** | `rig default`, without touching the workspace. |
| **R: Install Rtools** | Installs the Rtools versions your R versions need but do not have. |

A status bar item shows the workspace's R version and turns yellow when it differs from `renv.lock`. Click it to switch. That pairs well with the [project template](https://github.com/OndrejMottl/Project_template), which uses renv.

The extension writes the same settings as the manual method below, using rig's version link when it exists, including `r.rpath.windows` when R Debugger is installed. Restart the R terminal after switching. It does not set `QUARTO_R` (version 1.2.0), so `quarto render` needs the [separate step for Quarto](#quarto-render).

### By hand

First, once per machine, create the version-named shortcuts:

```powershell
rig system make-links   # creates R-4.6.2.exe, R-4.5.1.exe, ... in C:\Program Files\R\bin
```

Then in the project's `.vscode/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "r.executablePath": "R-4.5.1.exe",
  "r.consoleArgs": ["--no-save", "--no-restore", "--r-binary=R-4.5.1.exe"],
  "r.rpath.windows": "R-4.5.1.exe"
}
```

- `r.executablePath` is the R that vscode-R uses for the language server, help and the workspace viewer.
- `r.consoleArgs` is passed to radian. `--r-binary` makes radian start that R. The first two arguments are vscode-R's default, which the workspace value would otherwise replace.
- `r.rpath.windows` is for the R Debugger extension, which reads only this older setting. Without it, the debugger runs the default R instead of the pinned one. vscode-R marks the setting as deprecated, but asks to keep it, with the same value as `r.executablePath`, while R Debugger is installed. Leave it out if you do not use R Debugger.
- `R-4.5.1.exe` is found on `PATH`, so the file contains no user name and no install path. It works on every machine that has R 4.5.1 through rig, so the file can be committed.
- Keep the `.exe`. vscode-R adds `.exe` only to names without an extension, and `R-4.5.1` looks like it has one (`.1`), so without it vscode-R does not find R. radian accepts both.
- A full path such as `C:\\Program Files\\R\\R-4.5.1\\bin\\R.exe` also works and contains no user name, but it is Windows-only.

To check which R a terminal really runs: `R.version.string` in the console, or `radian --r-binary=R-4.5.1 --version` in PowerShell.

### Quarto projects {#quarto-render}

The `.vscode/settings.json` pin reaches only vscode-R and radian. `quarto render` does not read it: it uses the `Rscript` on `PATH`, which is rig's default. In a project with renv that shows up as missing packages, because renv keeps a separate project library for each R version (`renv/library/windows/R-4.x/...`), and the default R looks in the wrong one ([symptom](troubleshooting.qmd#quarto-render-cannot-find-installed-packages)).

To pin Quarto as well, set `QUARTO_R` in a file called `_environment.local` at the root of the Quarto project:

```
QUARTO_R="C:/Program Files/R/R-4.5.1/bin"
```

and keep the file out of git, because the path is machine-specific. In `.gitignore`:

```
_environment.local
```

- The value is the R install's `bin` folder, not rig's `R-4.5.1.exe` shortcut. Quarto looks for `Rscript.exe` in the folder it is given, and next to the shortcut, in `C:\Program Files\R\bin`, that is rig's default again. (I have not tried the shortcut; I expect it to fail for that reason.)
- `QUARTO_R` set in the shell, or in a committed `_environment`, works too, but `_environment.local` keeps the path out of the repository.
- Lines starting with `#` are comments, so the file can say why it is there.
